title: Love and grief
hook: grief is love with nowhere to go, as many say

segments.voice: Yesterday, shema, listening as love: Job's friends sitting on the ground in silence. Your line was just listen. Who did you let finish? Today stays close to that silence, with a harder kind of love. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

A coat still hangs by the door, months later. Nobody wears it. Nobody can move it either. A phone still holds a voicemail that never gets deleted. A recipe card sits in a drawer in handwriting that won't come again. These are small things, and they can stop a person cold in the middle of an ordinary afternoon. People sometimes put it this way: grief is love with nowhere to go. In the Gospel of John, there's a scene where grief and love show up together, side by side, in the same breath. Today: love and grief.
screen: `A COAT STILL BY THE DOOR.` → `A VOICEMAIL NEVER DELETED.` → `GRIEF AND LOVE, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the scene. Jesus has a friend named Lazarus, in the village of Bethany, with his sisters Martha and Mary. Lazarus falls sick and dies before Jesus arrives. When Jesus comes, Mary falls at his feet weeping, and the people with her are weeping too. Jesus asks where they have laid him. And then comes a verse of two words, in the King James text: "Jesus wept." Second, what the onlookers see. They don't say, look how sad he is. The text has them say, "Behold how he loved him!" Standing by a grave, they read his tears as love. That's the whole idea of today in one line: the grief was the shape the love took. Third, the surprise. In John's story, Jesus is about to call Lazarus out of the tomb. The ending is close. And still he weeps. Some Christians see in it that hope doesn't cancel grief. Even with a happy ending moments away, the loss is real and it's honored with tears. Fourth, the idea from the hook. Grief is love with nowhere to go. It's a line people say, not a scripture, but it fits the scene. Love that used to have a phone number, a chair at the table, a person to reach. Now it has nowhere to land, so it comes out as tears, as a coat that can't be moved. Seen this way, grief isn't a sign that something went wrong with you. It's evidence of what was there. Different traditions hold death and what follows it in very different ways, and this lesson won't choose among them. But on any path, the tears can be read the way the people at Bethany read them.
screen: `A FRIEND NAMED LAZARUS.` · `BEHOLD HOW HE LOVED HIM.` · `HE WEEPS ANYWAY.` · `LOVE WITH NOWHERE TO GO.` · then, large: `JESUS WEPT.`

segments.voice: Let the breath move at its own pace. If it feels right today, bring to mind one grief. It might be a person, or a place, a pet, a time of life, a friendship that ended. If nothing comes, that's fine too: just sit with the breath. If something does come, let it be there without fixing it. Then, quietly, say to yourself: it was love. Let that sentence sit beside the grief, not replacing it. If tears come, let them. If you pray, you can hold this one in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Bethany. The village where Lazarus died, and where the onlookers watched Jesus weep and said, behold how he loved him. Today's word.
Your line: it was love. Today, if an old loss catches you off guard, don't scold yourself for it. Name it for what it is, and let it be a kind of remembering. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Traditions mark grief in their own ways: Jewish mourners sit shiva, Christians hold funerals and remember the dead in prayer, Muslims pray the funeral prayer and visit the family, Hindus and Sikhs each hold their own rites and recitations for the departed, and many Buddhists chant and make offerings in their name.

fork.setup: you're standing with the crowd at Bethany, and you see Jesus weeping at his friend's grave. what do the people say?
fork.reveal: the text has them say, "behold how he loved him!" his tears are read as love. some others there ask whether he couldn't have kept his friend from dying.

original.note: Greek: he wept, shed tears, the verb in John 11:35.

trapdoor: what you thought: grief means something went wrong.
what it means: grief is the shape love takes when the person isn't there to receive it.
what a scholar hears: in John 11, Jesus weeps just before he calls Lazarus from the tomb, and the onlookers read the tears as love.

notes: 'Grief is love with nowhere to go' is presented as a saying people use, not a scripture; it's a modern line with uncertain authorship and is not attributed to anyone.

The onlookers in John 11:36 are 'the Jews' in the KJV; the script says 'the onlookers' / 'the people' to keep the focus on the scene. John 11:37 has some asking why he couldn't have prevented the death; the fork reveal mentions it.
Practice is optional ('if it feels right today') because grief may be raw for some listeners.
